summary.heading: Rigid bodies and torque
summary.html:
• A rigid body has size and shape but never deforms. It can translate (every point moves the same way) and rotate about an axis (every point turns through the same angle), or both (rolling).
  • For linear motion, treat the mass as concentrated at the centre of mass (at the centre of a uniform, symmetrical body; no calculation needed). A force through the centre of mass causes no rotation.
$$\tau = Fr\sin\theta$$
  • $r$ = distance from the axis to where the force acts; $\theta$ = angle between the force and $r$. Equivalently, force × perpendicular distance to its line of action.
  • Unit: N m (never J: torque is not energy).
  • Largest when $F$ is perpendicular to $r$; zero when the line of action passes through the axis.
  • Torques have a sense: choose clockwise or anticlockwise as positive.
  • A couple (equal, opposite, non-collinear forces) gives no resultant force but a resultant torque: rotation without linear acceleration.

summary.heading: Equilibrium
summary.html:
• A rigid body is in equilibrium only if both conditions hold:
$$\sum F = 0 \qquad \sum \tau = 0$$
  • Rotational equilibrium: total clockwise torque = total anticlockwise torque, about any axis.
  • Take torques about a point an unknown force passes through, so it drops out. Then use $\sum F = 0$ for the rest.
  • Include the weight of the beam or plank itself, acting at its centre.

summary.heading: Describing rotation
summary.html:
• Angular displacement $\Delta\theta$ (rad), angular velocity $\omega = \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$ ($\text{rad s}^{-1}$), angular acceleration $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$ ($\text{rad s}^{-2}$). Used with a sense, not as vectors.
  • A point at radius $r$: $v = \omega r$ and tangential acceleration $a = \alpha r$.
  • For constant $\alpha$, the A.1 equations carry over:
$$\Delta\theta = \frac{\omega_f + \omega_i}{2}\,t \qquad \omega_f = \omega_i + \alpha t$$ $$\Delta\theta = \omega_i t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 \qquad \omega_f^2 = \omega_i^2 + 2\alpha\Delta\theta$$
  • Graphs: gradient of $\theta$–$t$ is $\omega$; gradient of $\omega$–$t$ is $\alpha$, and its area is $\Delta\theta$.
  • Revolutions = $\Delta\theta / 2\pi$. Always work in radians.

summary.heading: Moment of inertia and Newton's second law for rotation
summary.html:
$$I = \sum mr^2 \qquad \tau = I\alpha$$
  • Moment of inertia ($\text{kg m}^2$) measures resistance to changes in angular velocity. It depends on the mass and how it is distributed about the axis: doubling $r$ makes $I$ four times bigger.
  • Formulas for solid shapes are given when needed, e.g. ring $MR^2$, solid disc $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$, solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$. A rod has a larger $I$ about its end than its centre.
  • An unbalanced torque gives an angular acceleration; $\tau$ and $I$ must be about the same axis.
  • Mass on a string round a pulley: write $mg - T = ma$ for the mass, $TR = I\alpha$ for the pulley, and link them with $a = \alpha R$ (no slipping).

summary.heading: Angular momentum and angular impulse
summary.html:
$$L = I\omega \qquad \Delta L = \tau\Delta t = \Delta(I\omega)$$
  • Unit of $L$: $\text{kg m}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}$.
  • Conservation: total angular momentum is constant unless a resultant external torque acts.
  • If $I$ changes, $\omega$ changes so that $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$: skaters pull their arms in to spin faster, divers tuck, collapsing stars spin up into fast neutron stars.
  • Kinetic energy is not conserved: a skater pulling in her arms gains $E_k$ from the work her muscles do. Bodies that couple together (a disc dropped onto a turntable) lose $E_k$, like a perfectly inelastic collision.
  • Angular impulse = area under the torque–time graph = change in angular momentum.

summary.heading: Rotational kinetic energy and rolling
summary.html:
$$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2I}$$
  • Work done by a torque, $\tau\Delta\theta$, changes the rotational kinetic energy.
  • Rolling without slipping: $v = \omega R$, and $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$.
  • Rolling down a slope, the lost $E_p$ is shared between translation and rotation, so a rolling body is slower than a frictionless sliding one. Larger $I$ for its mass and radius means slower: solid sphere beats solid cylinder beats hoop, whatever their masses and sizes.
  • Static friction makes rolling possible but does no work (the contact point is momentarily at rest).

summary.heading: Linear and rotational twins
summary.html:
LinearRotational
$s$, $v$, $a$$\Delta\theta$, $\omega$, $\alpha$
mass $m$moment of inertia $I = \sum mr^2$
force $F$torque $\tau = Fr\sin\theta$
$F = ma$$\tau = I\alpha$
$p = mv$$L = I\omega$
$F\Delta t = \Delta p$$\tau\Delta t = \Delta L$
$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{p^2}{2m}$$E_k = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2I}$

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Using the distance along the object instead of the perpendicular distance to the line of action (remember $\sin\theta$).
  • Writing torque in joules.
  • Forgetting the weight of the beam itself.
  • Checking only one equilibrium condition.
  • Using $r$ instead of $r^2$ in $I = \sum mr^2$, or measuring $r$ from the wrong point.
  • Using degrees in $v = \omega r$ or the rotational equations of motion.
  • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved when $I$ changes or bodies couple together.
  • Leaving out the rotational kinetic energy of a rolling body.

Models: When is the point-particle model good enough, and when do you need the rigid body? Try a thrown ball, a spinning top, a door and a planet.
The rigid-body model ignores bending. Ask students for a real object where that assumption fails (a diving board, a bridge, a golf club).
Patterns: Give students the linear column of the summary table and ask them to predict the rotational column before showing it.
Where does the analogy break down? (For example, $I$ depends on the axis chosen, but mass doesn't.)
Global impact: Flywheels store energy as $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. Why would an engineer make the rim heavy and spin it fast?
Which everyday tools are levers designed for a large torque from a small force (spanners, scissors, door handles, bottle openers)?

oracy.html:
Hot seat (whole class, 8 minutes): one student, the expert, answers the class's questions; swap experts every few questions. Situation: a spinning skater pulls her arms in and spins faster. Her angular momentum is conserved, yet her rotational kinetic energy increases. Where does the extra energy come from?

  • My question for the expert is …
  • Could you explain why …?
  • What would happen if …?

Listen for: $L = I\omega$ stays constant as $I$ falls, and her muscles do work pulling her arms inwards.

Is any model permanent?: The point particle was "replaced" but is still used every day. Is a model ever truly discarded, or just given a smaller job?
Compare with other areas of knowledge: do historians or economists keep using older models in the same way?
Does an analogy explain anything?: Does knowing that $\tau = I\alpha$ looks like $F = ma$ help you understand rotation, or just remember the equation?
Can an analogy mislead? Ask students for an example from another subject where it did.
What does \"rigid\" mean?: No real object is perfectly rigid. How would you decide whether a ruler, a car tyre or a skater counts as rigid for a given question?
Is knowledge built on an idealisation less certain than knowledge built on direct measurement?
Who owns an idea?: Archimedes' law of the lever is over 2000 years old and still in exams. What makes some ideas last so long?
If an idea is refined many times by many people, whose idea is the final version?

videos.use: A short review of angular momentum and its conservation. Use it for revision, or set it before the lesson on $L = I\omega$.

videos.title: Rotational Inertia: The Race Between a Ring and a Disc
videos.channel: North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics
videos.use: A ring and a disc race down a ramp. Pause before the result and ask students to predict the winner using energy sharing between translation and rotation.

videos.title: NASA | What is a Pulsar?
videos.use: Pulsars are collapsed stars spinning many times a second. Ask students to explain the fast spin with conservation of angular momentum as the star's radius shrinks.
